items.stem: An agent spends $0.12 per attempt on model calls and $0.03 per attempt on tools. In a week, 10,000 attempts, including re-runs, complete 7,500 tasks. What is the cost per completed task?

options.feedback: This is the model spend of one attempt. It leaves out tool fees and ignores the attempts that did not complete a task.
This is the full cost of one attempt, but it divides by attempts. The 2,500 failed attempts still cost money and must be carried by the completed tasks.
Correct. Spend is 10,000 times $0.15, or $1,500, and $1,500 divided by 7,500 completed tasks is $0.20.
This divides model spend alone by completed tasks. Tool and retrieval fees are part of what a task costs, so they belong in the total.

items.explanation: Add every model and tool cost across all attempts, including failures and re-runs, then divide by the tasks that succeed.

items.stem: Order these prompt sections for the best cache hit rate, from the start of the prompt to the end.

items.text: The conversation so far, which grows every turn.
System instructions and tool definitions, which change only on deploy.
The user's latest message, which is new on every call.
The review rubric, which changes about once a month.
The customer's account profile, which is fixed for the whole session.

items.explanation: The cache matches a prefix from the start, so order sections from most stable to least stable. Anything that changes invalidates every section after it.

items.stem: Caching was enabled a month ago, but the cache-read token count is near zero on every call. Which change most likely explains it?

options.text: The system prompt now starts with the current date and time.
options.feedback: Correct. The first bytes differ on every call, so no prefix ever matches and every call pays to write the cache.

options.text: The user's messages have become longer.
options.feedback: Not the cause. User messages sit after the cache breakpoint, so their length does not affect whether the prefix matches.

options.text: Traffic doubled during business hours.
options.feedback: More traffic keeps the cache warmer, not colder. Busy periods should raise cache reads.

options.text: The output cap was lowered from 1,000 to 600 tokens.
options.feedback: Output length has no effect on prefix matching. It changes output spend, not cache hits.

items.explanation: Timestamps, request IDs, unsorted JSON and reordered tools silently break the prefix match. Cache-read token counts are how you catch it.

items.stem: Moving the planning step to a model at a fifth of the price cuts cost per attempt by 30 per cent, but task success falls from 0.95 to 0.70. Failures are re-run. What should you conclude?

options.text: Ship it, because the cost per attempt fell by 30 per cent.
options.feedback: The attempt price is the wrong measure. Re-runs and lost tasks are part of the cost, and success fell by 25 points.

options.text: Reject it for planning: cost per completed task barely falls, and success drops far below the floor.
options.feedback: Correct. If an attempt cost $0.10, a completed task cost about $0.105 before and $0.07 divided by 0.70, or $0.10, after. That 5 per cent saving costs 25 points of success.

options.text: Route every step to the cheaper model, so the saving is larger.
options.feedback: That spreads the quality loss to every step. Planning is a hard step; cheaper models suit easy steps such as classification and extraction.

options.text: Keep the change but raise the retry limit until success recovers.
options.feedback: More retries spend the saving and add latency. Fix the route instead of paying to retry a model that is wrong for the step.

items.explanation: Judge routes by cost per completed task and task success on a golden set. A cheaper call that fails more often is not cheaper.

items.stem: An agent's context reaches 40,000 tokens by step 10. Which changes trim it while protecting task success? Select all that apply.

options.text: Summarise each long tool observation and keep an ID so the full text can be fetched again.
options.feedback: Correct. The summary carries the facts forward, and the ID lets a later step recover detail if it needs it.

options.text: Cap retrieval to the top few passages, chosen by relevance score.
options.feedback: Correct. Low-ranked passages add tokens and noise, and the golden set shows whether the cap loses answers.

options.text: Drop the whole history after every step.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The agent loses the facts and decisions it needs to finish, so success falls and re-runs rise.

options.text: Drop turns that no longer affect the current decision, keeping the last few verbatim.
options.feedback: Correct. Stale history costs tokens on every call while adding nothing to the next step.

options.text: Cap output at 100 tokens for every step, including the structured verdict.
options.feedback: Incorrect. A cap below the real output size truncates verdicts, causing parse failures and retries that cost more than they save.

items.explanation: Trim what the next step does not need, keep a way back to full detail, and size caps from the real output distribution. Confirm on the golden set.

items.stem: Which workload is the best candidate for a batch API at roughly half price?

options.text: Live chat replies to customers on the support site.
options.feedback: A person is waiting for each reply, and batch results can take hours. Keep this interactive.

options.text: Grading 50,000 agent transcripts from the previous day for a morning quality report.
options.feedback: Correct. Nobody waits for any single result, and the report is needed by morning, so a batch window of hours fits.

options.text: Tool calls that check stock levels during checkout.
options.feedback: Checkout is blocked until the call returns, so a delay of hours would break the purchase.

options.text: Routing an inbound email to a queue while the sender waits for an acknowledgement.
options.feedback: The acknowledgement depends on the routing decision, so it cannot wait hours for a batch result.

items.explanation: Batch suits work nobody is waiting for: evaluations, grading, backfills and periodic re-checks.

items.stem: A route's trailing median cost is $0.20 per request, and alerts fire at three times the median. Which request should raise an alert?

options.text: A request costing $0.35.
options.feedback: Below the threshold. At $0.35 it is 1.75 times the median, which is ordinary variation for a loop.

options.text: A request costing $0.55.
options.feedback: Close, but $0.55 is 2.75 times the median. The threshold is $0.60.

options.text: A request costing $0.72.
options.feedback: Correct. Three times $0.20 is $0.60, and $0.72 is 3.6 times the median, so it alerts with its trace, tenant and model.

options.text: None, because alerts should be based on the monthly invoice.
options.feedback: A runaway loop can spend a month's budget in hours. Per-request alerts catch it long before an invoice does.

items.explanation: A multiple of the trailing median adapts to each route's normal cost, so one threshold rule works across cheap and expensive routes.

items.stem: A tenant has spent its whole monthly budget with a week to go. Which responses fit good cost guardrails? Select all that apply.

options.text: Route the tenant's calls to a smaller model and tell users the service is in a reduced mode.
options.feedback: Correct. This is a degradation rung: service continues at lower cost, and users know which mode they are in.

options.text: Return an error on every request until the next month.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Failing outright is the worst rung. Degrade first, and stop only if no cheaper mode is acceptable.

options.text: Serve exemplar answers only for common questions and queue the rest.
options.feedback: Correct. Exemplars and queued work keep useful service running with little or no model spend.

options.text: Group the tenant's spend by route and model to find what drove it.
options.feedback: Correct. Attribution shows whether one route, one model or a runaway loop caused the overspend, which guides the fix.

options.text: Quietly switch to a weaker model without telling anyone.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Silent degradation erodes trust and hides the drop in quality from reports. Show and record the current rung.

items.explanation: Budgets should trigger a visible step down the degradation ladder, and attribution should explain where the money went.

items.stem: Put the steps for safely moving an extraction step to a cheaper model in order.

items.text: Compare quality on the route and cost per completed task against the baseline.
Build a golden set of real extraction cases with known answers.
Roll out to a small share of traffic and watch task success.
Measure the current model's quality and cost on the golden set.
Run the cheaper model on the same golden set.

items.explanation: You need fixed cases before any measurement, a baseline before a comparison, and a passing comparison before any live traffic sees the new route.

items.stem: A team's dashboard shows cost per model request. Which problem would it most likely hide?

options.text: A loop that now takes 9 calls per task instead of 6.
options.feedback: Correct. Each request costs the same, so the dashboard stays flat while the bill per task rises by half.

options.text: A switch to a provider with higher token prices.
options.feedback: A price rise shows up directly in cost per request, so this dashboard would catch it.

options.text: A prompt change that doubles input tokens on every call.
options.feedback: Each request carries the extra tokens, so cost per request rises visibly.

options.text: Longer outputs on every call after a format change.
options.feedback: Longer outputs raise the cost of each request, so this dashboard would show it.

items.explanation: Cost per request misses changes in how many calls, retries and re-runs a task needs. Track cost per completed task as the headline number.
